newsitem.title: USA: New York tightens security after bomb raid.
newsitem.headline: New York tightens security after bomb raid.

text.p: Security was tightened around New York on Friday, a day after authorities said they had foiled an alleged plot by Middle Eastern men to attack the city's subway system with a suicide bomb.

Two men charged in the alleged conspiracy were shot and wounded by police in a dawn raid on Thursday in which five pipe bombs were discovered in a ramshackle Brooklyn apartment. The devices were safely removed. A third man is being questioned by agents from the Joint Terrorist Task Force of local, state and federal agencies, officials said.

Authorities said at least one of two suspects named in court documents had a Jordanian passport. They said Gazi Ibrahim Abu Mezer, 23, had allegedly been accused in Israel "of being a member of a known terrorist organisation."

The other suspect named in a complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Brooklyn was identified as Lafi Khalil, 22. Both were in a hospital on Friday recovering from surgery for gunshot wounds suffered in the police raid.

The security concerns in the city were reminiscent of the aftermath of the February 1993 bombing of the World Trade Centre by Moslem militants in which six people were killed and more than 1,000 injured.

Major subway, regional rail and bus stations, government buildings, courthouses, diplomatic offices, synagogues and mosques were among the places where police officers and security guards were seen in greater numbers.

"There are extra police and extra patrols in places that the police department and the FBI might consider sensitive areas ... I would not call it an alert," New York Mayor Rudolph Giuliani told WCBS News in a radio interview.
Giuliani, police and FBI officials were to hold a news conference at 1:30 p.m. EDT (1730 GMT) Friday, a spokeswoman for the mayor said.
In Washington, President Bill Clinton praised police but said it was too early to draw conclusions about the case.

"We have worked very hard in this country to increase our capacity to deal with terrorism, it is something we take very seriously, and we will continue to do that," Clinton told reporters at the White House.

Authorities said there appeared to be no evidence directly linking the men arrested in New York with Wednesday's double suicide bombing of a Jerusalem market by the militant Palestinian group Hamas that killed 13 people and wounded 170.
But officials said the suspects intended to target Americans and Jews.
"It looks like they were going to set off a suicide bomb and try to make the point that the United States and Israel are wrong and strike against U.S. and Jewish interests," Giuliani said on Friday.

A man living in the same apartment tipped police officers about the explosives on Wednesday night, police sources said. They said that he told officers his roommates were planning to bomb a subway train or a bus in New York.

The head of the FBI office in New York, James Kallstrom, told WBZ-AM radio in Boston that they foiled the plot within 24 hours of when the bombs were to have been exploded. Asked "how close that event was to being pulled off?" Kallstrom replied. "Pretty close. I think less than a day."

Four of the devices removed from the apartment by police bomb disposal experts were pipe bombs strapped together and they contained black powder or nails with wires and switches, according to police sources.
The court documents said Abu Mezer gave police instructions on how to detonate or disarm the bombs. "He indicated that the bombs were targeted for detonation on the subway."
The charges against Abu Mezer and Khalil included conspiracy to damage and destroy buildings and vehicles with explosives.
In the West Bank, relatives said the two men had gone to the United States to live the "American Dream."
"His great dream was to go to America and live there... His ambition was to live happily, that's all," said Khalil's uncle, Suheil Mifleh Khalil.
Abu Mezer's brother, Nur, said they had last spoken by telephone a week ago.
"He was thanking the American people who are hospitable, who have freedom. Is it possible that a person who says such things would harm them?" asked Nur, a lawyer in the West Bank town of Hebron.
